title: 1 Chronicles 15:1–15
context: 1 Chronicles 15:1–15 describes David’s preparation for the second, successful attempt to bring up the ark. This material is largely Chronicles’ own; 2 Samuel 6:12–13 speaks briefly of “those who bore the LORD’s ark” without describing the Levites. David pitches a tent for the ark, declares that only the Levites may carry it (compare Deuteronomy 10:8), gathers the priests and Levites by their families, and tells them to sanctify themselves. In 15:13 he explains the earlier disaster: the ark had not been carried by the Levites, and “we didn’t seek him according to the ordinance.” The Levites then carry the ark on their shoulders with its poles, as Moses commanded (Exodus 25:14; Numbers 7:9). Several of the family heads belong to the clans of Kohath: Elizaphan, Hebron, and Uzziel are Kohathite family names (Exodus 6:18, 22; Numbers 3:27–30). Both traditions read the section as shared ground: obedience to God’s word and joy in his presence belong together, and failure can lead to renewed and corrected worship.

verses.text: David made himself houses in David’s city; and he prepared a place for God’s ark, and pitched a tent for it.
verses.arminianNotes:
David builds houses for himself in David’s city, prepares a place for God’s ark, and pitches a tent for it. This time preparation comes before the procession.

Arminian readers see a king who has learned from failure and now plans with care, and they note that repentance often shows itself in changed practice rather than in words alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this tent is distinct from the tabernacle, which 16:39 places at the high place at Gibeon (compare 2 Chronicles 1:3–4), and they see God’s presence being given a fitting place at the center of David’s kingdom.

Both traditions read the verse as patient and reverent preparation for worship and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: Then David said, “No one ought to carry God’s ark but the Levites. For the LORD has chosen them to carry God’s ark, and to minister to him forever.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David declares, “No one ought to carry God’s ark but the Levites.” He explains that the LORD chose them to carry the ark and to minister to him forever. This matches the law that “the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to bear the ark of the LORD’s covenant” (Deuteronomy 10:8).

Arminian readers see David returning to God’s revealed word after the disaster.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that worship is governed by God’s appointment rather than human invention. The choosing here concerns an office of service given to a tribe, and neither tradition builds a doctrine of individual salvation on it.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God has made known how his presence is to be approached, and faithful worship follows that word.

verses.text: David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem, to bring up the LORD’s ark to its place, which he had prepared for it.
verses.arminianNotes:
David assembles all Israel at Jerusalem to bring up the LORD’s ark to the place he has prepared for it. The whole people is involved again.

Arminian readers see a renewed invitation to the entire nation after the failure of the first attempt, and they note that God’s people may begin again in obedience after a painful lesson has been learned.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the phrase about the place he had prepared for it, and they see God’s presence being approached in an ordered way, with the place, the carriers, and the people all made ready beforehand.

Both traditions read the gathering as a sign that worship belongs to the whole covenant community and that obedience and joy can be restored together.

verses.text: David gathered together the sons of Aaron and the Levites:
verses.arminianNotes:
David gathers the sons of Aaron and the Levites. The priests and the Levites each have their part in what follows.

Arminian readers note that David involves those God appointed for this service, and they see the gathering as an act of faithful obedience in which each group must willingly take up its own responsibility before the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this gathering of priests and Levites is part of Chronicles’ own material on the Levites, which 2 Samuel 6 does not include, and they see it as evidence of the Chronicler’s concern that worship be ordered according to God’s appointment.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the place of appointed ministers in Israel’s worship.

verses.text: of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief, and his brothers one hundred twenty;
verses.arminianNotes:
Of the sons of Kohath, Uriel is the chief, with one hundred twenty of his brothers. The Kohathites were the family charged with carrying the holy things (Numbers 4:15).

Arminian readers find it fitting that the Kohathites are listed first, since the earlier disaster came from neglecting their appointed role, and they see faithful service restored through willing and prepared servants.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the numbering of the Kohathites recalls the arrangements of the wilderness (Numbers 3:27–31), showing continuity between Moses’ ordinances and David’s worship. God’s order for his house is not reinvented but received.

Both traditions read the verse as a careful record of real servants of God and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: of the sons of Merari, Asaiah the chief, and his brothers two hundred twenty;
verses.arminianNotes:
Of the sons of Merari, Asaiah is the chief, with two hundred twenty of his brothers. Merari was one of Levi’s three sons (Exodus 6:16).

Arminian readers note that each Levitical family has its own leader and its own number, and they see the list as honoring the many ordinary people who give themselves to serving God in the community of his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the list the orderly structure of Israel’s worship, in which each family’s place reflects God’s arrangement rather than human preference, and they note that the Merarites, too, share in bringing up the ark.

Both traditions read the verse as historical record that honors faithful service and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: of the sons of Gershom, Joel the chief, and his brothers one hundred thirty;
verses.arminianNotes:
Of the sons of Gershom, Joel is the chief, with one hundred thirty of his brothers. Elsewhere the name usually appears as Gershon (Exodus 6:16), and Chronicles also uses the spelling Gershom in 6:43.

Arminian readers see all three branches of Levi taking part, and they note that no family is left out of the work of restoring the LORD’s ark to its proper place.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the participation of Kohath, Merari, and Gershom shows the whole tribe of Levi acting together under the ordinance given through Moses, so that the procession is a renewal of covenant order rather than a new invention.

Both traditions read the verse as a record of willing and ordered service and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah the chief, and his brothers two hundred;
verses.arminianNotes:
Of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah is the chief, with two hundred of his brothers. Elizaphan the son of Uzziel had been prince of the Kohathite families (Numbers 3:30; compare Exodus 6:22, where the name is Elzaphan).

Arminian readers see family histories of faithful service continuing across generations, as descendants take up the calling of their ancestors with renewed devotion.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Kohathite line is represented by several of its families, which underlines the care taken to correct the earlier failure by placing the ark in the hands of those God appointed to carry it.

Both traditions read the verse as historical record and as part of Chronicles’ attention to the Levites, and they treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: of the sons of Hebron, Eliel the chief, and his brothers eighty;
verses.arminianNotes:
Of the sons of Hebron, Eliel is the chief, with eighty of his brothers. Hebron here is a family name, a son of Kohath (Exodus 6:18), not the city.

Arminian readers note that even a smaller family has its place in the work, and they see the list as an encouragement that no service offered to God is too small to be remembered and honored by him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Hebronites are another Kohathite family (Numbers 3:27), so that the bearers of the ark are drawn from the very clan the law had assigned to the holy things.

Both traditions read the verse as part of a careful record and treat it as shared ground about faithful, ordered service in the worship of Israel.

verses.text: of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, and his brothers one hundred twelve.
verses.arminianNotes:
Of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab is the chief, with one hundred twelve of his brothers. Uzziel was also a son of Kohath (Exodus 6:18).

Arminian readers note that the list closes with yet another family ready to serve, and they see the willingness of these households as a contrast with the improvised arrangements of the first attempt in chapter 13, when the Levites had no clear part.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that four of the six groups named belong to Kohath’s line, which reflects the law’s assignment of the ark and the holy things to the Kohathites (Numbers 4:15; 7:9).

Both traditions read the list as showing that the second procession is carefully grounded in God’s word and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: David called for Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and for the Levites: for Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab,
verses.arminianNotes:
David calls Zadok and Abiathar the priests, along with the Levite chiefs Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab. Priests and Levites are summoned together.

Arminian readers see shared leadership in worship, with each leader called to take personal responsibility for leading the people faithfully in what God has commanded.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Zadok and Abiathar will later take different paths, when Abiathar follows Adonijah and is removed from the priesthood (1 Kings 1:7; 2:27), and they see in this a reminder that God’s purposes continue through changing human leaders.

Both traditions read the verse as an orderly summons to the servants God had appointed.

verses.text: and said to them, “You are the heads of the fathers’ households of the Levites. Sanctify yourselves, both you and your brothers, that you may bring the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, up to the place that I have prepared for it.
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells them that they are the heads of the fathers’ households of the Levites and commands, “Sanctify yourselves,” so that they may bring up the ark of the LORD to the place he has prepared.

Arminian readers stress the leaders’ responsibility to prepare themselves, and they see consecration as a real act of obedience that God calls his servants to undertake willingly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that holiness is God’s requirement for those who approach him, and they see consecration as the means God appointed for coming near, a requirement that ultimately points to the holiness God himself supplies to his people.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: those who serve before God must come prepared and set apart for him.

verses.text: For because you didn’t carry it at first, the LORD our God broke out in anger against us, because we didn’t seek him according to the ordinance.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David explains, “because you didn’t carry it at first, the LORD our God broke out in anger against us, because we didn’t seek him according to the ordinance.”

Arminian readers note that David includes himself in the confession, using “us” and “we”, and they see honest repentance that takes responsibility for the failure instead of blaming Uzza alone, together with a resolve to do better.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see this as the key interpretive verse for the death of Uzza: the fault lay in failing to seek God according to his ordinance, so God’s judgment was neither arbitrary nor unexplained.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s holiness and the duty to approach him as he has commanded, and neither adds a contrast here.

verses.text: So the priests and the Levites sanctified themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests and the Levites sanctify themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel. They do what David asked.

Arminian readers see a willing and wholehearted response from those called to serve, and they note that the people’s readiness to obey after failure is itself a sign of renewed faith and a fitting answer to God’s patience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see obedience following instruction, and they note that the priests and Levites now act according to the word God gave through Moses rather than according to the improvised method of the first attempt.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about consecration that comes before service in God’s presence.

verses.text: The children of the Levites bore God’s ark on their shoulders with its poles, as Moses commanded according to the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Levites carry God’s ark on their shoulders with its poles, as Moses commanded according to the LORD’s word. The law had placed poles in the rings of the ark for this purpose (Exodus 25:14).

Arminian readers see the correction completed, and they see joy returning when God’s people choose to follow what he has said rather than their own ideas.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the phrase “as Moses commanded according to the LORD’s word” and note that the authority for the change is God’s word, not David’s preference, and that Chronicles’ account here fills in what 2 Samuel 6:13 implies by speaking of those who bore the ark.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about obedient worship.
